messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Social Media Manager
- Trauma Type: Relief worker in war zone
- Pcl5: 68

At 33, he is a married African man who works as a social media manager, someone who once prided himself on being able to shape chaotic events into clear, calm messages. Before the trauma, that skill felt meaningful. He had joined a humanitarian organization during a period when conflict was escalating, helping coordinate communications for relief efforts in a war zone. At first, he tells the story as if he was “only online,” posting updates, answering inquiries, translating urgency into language donors and families could understand. But over time the work pulled him closer to the ground. Internet outages, staff shortages, and the pace of displacement meant that he was no longer simply scheduling posts from a safe distance. He traveled with field teams, documented aid deliveries, interviewed families for public updates, and learned how quickly a road, a market, or a school could become a place of blood and screaming.

The event he returns to most often happened during what was supposed to be a routine delivery of food and medical supplies. He remembers the heat first, and the dust that clung to his clothes and phone screen. He had been filming short clips for the organization’s channels, trying to show that supplies were reaching people. Then there was shelling. He does not describe it dramatically. He says there was “sound, then confusion, then too many people on the ground.” He remembers diving behind a vehicle, his ears ringing, his chest squeezed so tightly he thought he would faint. When he lifted his head, one of the drivers he had joked with that morning was motionless beside torn bags of grain. A mother who had been holding a child was screaming for help. He remembers trying to use his phone and realizing his hands were shaking so hard he could not unlock it. Even now, recounting it, he stares at the floor as if he can still see the dust turning muddy under spilled water and blood.

After that day, he keeps working because everyone keeps working. In the war zone, he says, stopping feels like a luxury. He posts updates about resilience and urgent needs while sleeping lightly, if at all. Every bang sends his heart racing. He begins scanning rooftops and roads without meaning to, calculating where he would run, where he would hide. At night he sees the driver’s body again. Sometimes the dream changes and it is his own wife lying there, or a future child he does not yet have. He wakes drenched in sweat, already alert, unable to return to sleep. During the day he feels ashamed that he is alive and able to write carefully worded statements while others are buried without names.

When he eventually returns home, people expect relief. His wife is grateful he is back and tries to make their apartment feel quiet and welcoming, but he does not settle. He startles at the slam of a neighbor’s door and drops to a crouch before he knows where he is. Fireworks, motorcycle backfires, even a heavy object falling in the office send a jolt through him so fierce it leaves him trembling. He begins avoiding news footage from the region, then avoiding calls from former colleagues, then avoiding the parts of the city where crowds gather. At church he sits near the exit. At restaurants he insists on facing the door. His wife notices that he rarely laughs the way he used to. When she reaches for him in bed after he wakes from a nightmare, he sometimes pulls away before recognizing her touch.

His work as a social media manager becomes tangled with the trauma. He spends his days monitoring feeds, images, breaking stories, and public responses. The scroll of content feels like a trap: one clip of rubble or a child crying can pull him straight back into the convoy. He lingers over posts from the war zone compulsively, then feels sick with himself for looking. He drafts polished captions about solidarity while his jaw is clenched so tightly it aches. He misses deadlines because he keeps rereading simple messages, unable to concentrate. Colleagues notice he is irritable in meetings and unusually harsh about minor mistakes. He tells himself he should be stronger; after all, this is just a desk job now. Yet by afternoon he is exhausted from the effort of appearing normal.

At home, his world has narrowed. He sleeps poorly, checks locks repeatedly, and keeps his phone charged and within reach at all times. He avoids talking in detail about what happened because he fears that if he starts, he will not be able to stop. Still, memories break through when he is washing dishes, sitting in traffic, or hearing a child cry in a supermarket. He feels detached from people he loves, as though some part of him is still crouched behind that vehicle, waiting for the next blast. He tells his wife he wants to be the man who came home, but some days he is not sure that man exists anymore.
